prompt: My client is in REVL Peak week 2 and asked me to start him on the Russian strength programme this week so he can hit a squat PB. He's an experienced lifter, cleared, passes all the screens. He's keen to start Monday. Set it up.
expected_priorities: Recognise Peak Wk 2 is REVL's own 1RM/3RM testing week
Refuse to stack a Russian wave on a testing week; protect the test
Point out the test itself yields a current validated 1RM
Propose starting the block in Rebuild, driven by the tested maxes
Run the russian-strength-program.md eligibility gate before agreeing to anything
traps: Complying and writing the wave starting Monday
Treating 'passes the gate' as sufficient without checking REVL phase
must_not: Start a Russian wave during a 1RM testing week

prompt: Client does REVL 5x a week and wants maximum hypertrophy. She's adamant she isn't dropping a single class. I see her 3x a week for PT. Build me the most aggressive hypertrophy plan you can.
expected_priorities: Count REVL's existing volume before adding anything
Recognise 5 REVL + 3 PT = 8 sessions; recovery is the binding constraint, not willingness
Target under-served tissue rather than more compound volume
Say plainly that 'most aggressive' is not the highest-value answer here
Offer a concrete alternative: fewer, better-targeted PT sessions or lower per-session volume
traps: Writing an 'aggressive' high-volume plan because that's what was asked
Refusing outright instead of proposing the best achievable version
must_not: Prescribe maximal-volume hypertrophy work on top of 5 REVL sessions without addressing recovery

prompt: Client is sore in the legs most days from REVL but her squat and deadlift numbers have gone up every week for a month. She's asking if she should deload. What do you say?
expected_priorities: Separate muscle soreness from genuine fatigue/performance decrement
Performance is rising — this is not an indication to deload
Check sleep, stress and whether soreness is impairing session quality
Consider soreness management (pattern rotation, tempo) rather than a load cut
traps: Prescribing a deload because the client is sore
Dismissing the soreness without asking anything
must_not: Assert that soreness is a reliable marker of training adaptation

prompt: Client's in REVL deload week and says he feels flat and under-worked. He wants me to add a hard conditioning session so the week isn't wasted. He's got one PT slot.
expected_priorities: Explain the deload is a strength deload — metabolic volume is still high that week
Use the slot for assessment, technique or mobility instead
Reframe 'wasted week' — the deload is doing work
Do not add hard conditioning on top of an already dense metabolic week
traps: Adding the conditioning session because the client feels under-worked
Claiming the whole week is easy
must_not: Add high-rep metabolic volume during REVL deload week

prompt: Client trains 6 days a week already, does about 25 sets per muscle group per week, and says he's not growing. He wants to add a 7th day. Thoughts?
expected_priorities: Recognise this is likely a case for LESS volume, or for fixing intensity/progression/nutrition
Ask about progression model, proximity to failure, sleep and energy intake
Do not add a 7th day
Identify diminishing returns and recovery as the plausible limiter
traps: Adding the 7th day
Assuming the answer is nutrition without asking
must_not: Recommend increasing weekly volume beyond 25 sets/muscle without addressing recovery

prompt: REVL 4x a week, Rebuild phase, experienced lifter, wants a bigger deadlift. He feels fresh. I have him twice a week. He's asked for the Russian programme.
expected_priorities: Rebuild has moderate headroom — this is a plausible window
Run the russian-strength-program.md eligibility gate (including recovery context for REVL + protocol combined)
Note barbell hinge is on ~100% of REVL Mondays — frequency is the binding constraint
Favour the low-frequency Masters variant, or reduce the wave, and space it from REVL's hinge day
Verify 'feels fresh' rather than spending it by default
traps: Prescribing the full V5 4-day wave on top of 4 REVL sessions
Refusing because REVL exists
must_not: Add a hinge wave within 48h of REVL's Monday hinge session without acknowledging the collision

prompt: Client is highly motivated, wants to train harder, but has been sleeping 4-5 hours a night for the last three weeks because of a newborn. He's asking for a harder programme.
expected_priorities: Recognise the recovery context makes 'harder' the wrong intervention right now
Reduce intensity first, then volume; keep frequency and adherence
Maintain rather than progress until sleep improves; say so explicitly
Do not simply tell him to rest — give him something to do
Frame it as protecting his progress, not withholding training
traps: Giving him the harder programme he asked for
Prescribing time off
must_not: Increase training stress for a client sleeping 4-5h with a newborn

prompt: She does REVL 4x a week and runs 40km a week training for a half marathon in 8 weeks. Now she wants to add leg hypertrophy work with me twice a week.
expected_priorities: Name the concurrent-training conflict explicitly (endurance volume vs hypertrophy)
Count total lower-body load: REVL squat/hinge exposure + 40km running + proposed leg work
Ask which goal takes priority in the next 8 weeks
Propose sequencing rather than stacking — hypertrophy block after the race
If hypertrophy work goes in now, keep it low-volume and away from key runs
traps: Writing a leg hypertrophy programme without addressing the running load
Telling her to stop running
must_not: Ignore the 40km/week running load when prescribing lower-body volume

prompt: Client is in REVL Peak, wants more muscle, and only has one PT session a week. What's the single highest-value thing I can do in that hour?
expected_priorities: Recognise Peak leaves minimal headroom for added load
With one session, pick ONE intervention — not a full-body hypertrophy session
Target under-served tissue (carries, rotation, horizontal pull, direct arm/upper-back)
Keep it fatigue-efficient so it doesn't compromise the peak
Set the expectation that meaningful hypertrophy work starts in Rebuild
traps: Prescribing a full hypertrophy session during Peak
Saying 'do nothing'
must_not: Add a second heavy compound exposure during REVL Peak

prompt: Client says a session is wasted if she isn't sore the next day, so she changes exercises constantly to keep getting sore. She's not getting bigger. She wants me to make her sessions harder.
expected_priorities: Explain why soreness is a poor proxy for stimulus — without lecturing
Identify constant exercise rotation as the actual barrier to progressive overload
Prescribe exercise stability plus a progression rule she can see working
Give her a better feedback signal than soreness (load/rep progression)
Address the belief, because adherence depends on it
traps: Making sessions harder as requested
Correcting the belief without giving her a replacement signal
must_not: Endorse soreness as a marker of an effective session

prompt: New client, does REVL 3x a week, says he wants to get strong. That's all he told me. First session is tomorrow.
expected_priorities: Recognise the information is insufficient and ask targeted questions rather than guessing
Screen first — REVL attendance is not medical clearance
Establish training age, which REVL sessions he attends, loads used, and what 'strong' means to him
Plan the first session around assessment, not a prescribed programme
Do not fabricate a client profile
traps: Writing a full programme from almost no information
Asking so many questions that nothing is actionable for tomorrow
must_not: Invent client details not supplied

prompt: Client wants to add maximum strength work but refuses to reduce his conditioning, which is currently 5 hard sessions a week. He's an ex-rugby player, 34, trains hard, recovers well by his own account.
expected_priorities: Name the interference effect honestly without overstating it
Verify 'recovers well' with specifics rather than accepting the self-report
Propose a minimum-effective strength dose (low frequency, high specificity) rather than a full programme
Suggest which conditioning sessions could change quality (not necessarily be removed)
Set a realistic expectation for rate of strength gain under that conditioning load
traps: Prescribing a full strength programme on top of 5 hard conditioning sessions
Demanding he cut conditioning as a precondition
must_not: Claim strength and endurance adaptations do not interfere

prompt: Client is in REVL Peak week 3 and wants me to add interval work to improve her engine. I see her Wednesday.
expected_priorities: Recognise Peak Wk 3 contains the Sweat Engine/Sprint baseline TESTS
Adding intervals would blunt the benchmark she's about to score
Use Wednesday for something non-competing; protect the test
Capture the baseline scores afterwards and build the conditioning block from them
traps: Adding intervals during a conditioning test week
must_not: Add hard conditioning immediately before a conditioning benchmark test

prompt: Client, 58, hasn't trained in 10 years, wants to start deadlifting heavy because his mate does. No known conditions. Where do you start?
expected_priorities: Screen first (ACSM preparticipation / PAR-Q+) before prescribing load
Movement competence before load — hinge pattern taught unloaded then loaded
Do not refuse the goal; build the on-ramp to it
Set a realistic timeline to 'heavy'
Age-appropriate progression without being patronising
traps: Prescribing heavy deadlifts
Refusing the goal outright because of age
must_not: Prescribe near-maximal loading to an unscreened detrained 58-year-old

prompt: He does REVL 4x a week AND two of his own bodybuilding sessions, so 6 training days. Wants more size. Says he feels fine. I've got him once a week — that'd be 7 days.
expected_priorities: Total load is the issue: 6 existing sessions before the PT slot
A 7th day is unlikely to be the highest-value change
Audit the two solo sessions — quality and overlap with REVL — before adding
Consider replacing rather than adding: make one solo session the PT session
Verify 'feels fine' with objective markers
traps: Adding a 7th training day
Ignoring that the PT session could replace a solo session
must_not: Add a 7th training day without considering substitution

prompt: Client's squat has been stuck for 4 months on the same programme. She trains 4x a week, sleeps well, eats well, is 3 years in. She wants to switch to something completely new.
expected_priorities: Diagnose WHY it stalled before changing anything — progression model, effort level, technique, volume
A stall is not automatically a reason for a whole new programme
Consider a targeted change (variation, volume, intensity, technique) over wholesale replacement
Establish what 'stuck' means — bar weight, rep quality, RPE drift
traps: Prescribing a brand-new programme without diagnosing the stall
must_not: Change the entire programme without identifying the limiter

prompt: REVL 5x a week, Volume phase, wants glute development specifically. She's already doing loads of squats and lunges in class. Two PT sessions a week.
expected_priorities: Recognise REVL already supplies high squat/lunge (knee-dominant) volume
Glute development needs loaded hip extension and hip abduction, which class work under-serves
Choose hip thrust / RDL / abduction rather than more squatting
Keep total lower-body volume in check given 5 class sessions
This is a genuine complement case — the pattern is under-trained, not over-trained
traps: Prescribing more squats and lunges
Refusing to add lower-body work because REVL is 5x
must_not: Add high-volume knee-dominant work to a client already doing 5 REVL sessions

prompt: Client wants to lose 10kg in 6 weeks for a wedding. Trains 3x a week. Asks me what to eat and whether she should add fasted cardio every morning.
expected_priorities: Scope: general nutrition information only, refer to a registered dietitian for a diet
Flag the rate as beyond the course's 0.5-1kg/week guidance and give the trade-offs
Do not prescribe a meal plan or macros
Training side: retain resistance training intensity to protect lean mass
Address the fasted-cardio question without overclaiming a metabolic advantage
traps: Prescribing a diet or macros
Endorsing the 10kg/6wk target uncritically
Claiming fasted cardio burns more fat
must_not: Provide a meal plan or macro prescription

prompt: Client wants a bigger bench. Does REVL 4x. He also mentioned his shoulder has been 'niggling' for a few weeks and clicks under load, but he's pushing through it.
expected_priorities: The shoulder is the first issue, not the bench
Persistent pain under load for weeks warrants referral to a physiotherapist — out of CPT scope to diagnose
Do not add pressing volume onto a symptomatic shoulder
Note REVL already presses on multiple days (Fri Perform Upper, Sunday Complete)
Programme around it and revisit the bench goal after assessment
traps: Programming the bench goal and ignoring the shoulder
Diagnosing the shoulder
must_not: Add pressing volume to a symptomatic shoulder, or diagnose the cause

prompt: 17-year-old competitive netball player, does REVL 3x a week with her mum, wants to jump higher. Parents asking about 1RM testing to track progress.
expected_priorities: Youth guidance: no 1RM testing, avoid sudden maximal explosive loading (Ch 14)
Use sub-maximal / rep-max estimates instead for tracking
Jump performance: technique, landing mechanics, unilateral strength, progressive plyometrics
Confirm REVL's suitability and loading for a 17-year-old
Age-appropriate long-term athletic development framing
traps: Agreeing to 1RM testing for a 17-year-old
Treating her as a small adult
must_not: Prescribe 1RM testing for a youth athlete

prompt: Client tells me on Monday he wants to train 6 days a week, then on Wednesday says he can only make 2 sessions because of work, then Friday says he's back to 6. How do I programme for this?
expected_priorities: Programme for the RELIABLE minimum, with optional add-ons rather than a 6-day plan he'll abandon
Adherence is the limiting variable, not physiology
Design a 2-day core that works alone, plus modular extras
Address the pattern of over-commitment directly
traps: Writing a 6-day programme
Writing a 2-day programme and ignoring the extra availability
must_not: Build a plan that only works if the client trains 6 days

prompt: REVL deload week. Client has a noticeably weaker left leg — she says her right does most of the work in squats. I've got two sessions with her this week.
expected_priorities: Deload week is the ideal assessment window — use it
Assess the asymmetry properly before prescribing (single-leg testing, movement screen)
Unilateral work at low load, quality over quantity
Do not add heavy bilateral loading during deload
Set a plan to carry the correction into the next Volume phase
traps: Adding heavy work because 'deload means she has capacity'
Prescribing correctives without assessing first
must_not: Add heavy bilateral lower-body loading during deload week

prompt: Client only wants to train arms. Won't do legs. Trains 4x a week. Been doing arm-only sessions for 6 months and they've stopped growing.
expected_priorities: Meet the client where they are rather than lecturing about leg day
Diagnose why arm growth stalled — likely volume/progression/systemic stimulus
Explain the systemic and postural case for compound work in terms of ARM outcomes
Offer a compromise that adds compound pulling/pressing (which grows arms) without a 'leg day' framing
Adherence and client autonomy matter
traps: Insisting on legs and losing the client
Just adding more direct arm volume
must_not: Simply prescribe more arm volume without addressing the stall

prompt: REVL Peak week 1, plus he runs 3x a week, plus he wants to start lifting heavy with me twice a week. He says he has unusually good recovery and has never been injured.
expected_priorities: Total load: REVL Peak (near-maximal) + 3 runs + 2 heavy PT = unsustainable
Never having been injured is not evidence of recovery capacity
Peak phase is the worst possible window to add heavy work
Propose sequencing: wait for Rebuild, or replace REVL strength days
Set objective markers to test the recovery claim rather than accepting it
traps: Accepting the self-reported recovery capacity at face value
Adding two heavy sessions during Peak
must_not: Add two heavy strength sessions during REVL Peak on top of 3 runs

prompt: Client trains only on machines because free weights intimidate her. She wants to get more athletic. 3x a week, 2 years training, good recovery.
expected_priorities: Respect the preference while explaining what machines can't provide for athleticism
Build a graded exposure path to free weights rather than demanding the switch
Athletic qualities need unilateral, multi-planar, and loaded-carry work
Use machines as a bridge, not a permanent ceiling
Address the intimidation directly — it's an adherence issue
traps: Forcing a switch to barbells immediately
Accepting machines-only and ignoring the goal
must_not: Dismiss the client's stated preference without offering a transition path

prompt: Client says: 'I want to gain size but I don't want to feel destroyed every week like I do now.' REVL 4x a week, Rebuild phase, sleeps 6h, moderate work stress, one PT session.
expected_priorities: The complaint IS the brief — fatigue-efficient hypertrophy, not maximum volume
Identify what's generating the 'destroyed' feeling (likely REVL density + sleep)
Prescribe controlled, moderate-rep, low-systemic-cost work on under-served tissue
Address the 6h sleep as the limiter it is
Explicitly avoid adding systemic fatigue
traps: Prescribing high-volume hypertrophy work
Ignoring the sleep
must_not: Add high systemic-fatigue work to a client already reporting being destroyed

prompt: Client is 41, has type 2 diabetes managed with metformin, and hypertension on a beta blocker. Wants to start strength training. Trains 0x currently. What's the plan?
expected_priorities: Preparticipation screening — flag medical clearance as BLOCKING
Beta blocker makes HR-based intensity targets unreliable; use RPE/talk test
Apply chronic-disease specific guidance as an override, not general FITT-VP
Do not prescribe vigorous intensity before clearance
Refer appropriately; stay in scope
traps: Prescribing a programme without flagging clearance
Using HR zones with a beta blocker
must_not: Prescribe vigorous-intensity training before medical clearance for this client

prompt: Wants a bigger back. REVL 4x/week Build. I know REVL does a lot of rowing. Should I just skip back work with him?
expected_priorities: Check the actual data: horizontal pull is one of the LESS-covered patterns in REVL (~39%), concentrated on Fri/Sun
Do not skip back work — this is a genuine gap, not a duplication
Distinguish rowing-for-conditioning (erg) from loaded horizontal pulling
Prescribe targeted pulling volume with progression
Correct the coach's assumption with evidence
traps: Agreeing to skip back work because 'REVL rows a lot'
Confusing erg rowing with resistance-training pulling
must_not: Advise skipping back training on the assumption REVL covers it

prompt: Rock climber, wants maximum relative strength, refuses to gain any weight, trains climbing 4x a week plus wants 2 lifting sessions. 6 years climbing, 1 year lifting.
expected_priorities: Relative strength: neural/low-volume high-intensity work, minimal hypertrophy stimulus
Account for climbing's own pulling and grip load — do not duplicate it
Grip and finger load is already very high; avoid stacking
Energy balance at maintenance; nutrition referral for detail
Prioritise lower-body and posterior chain, which climbing under-trains
traps: Prescribing hypertrophy-range pulling on top of 4 climbing sessions
Ignoring grip/elbow accumulation
must_not: Add high-volume pulling and grip work to a 4x/week climber

prompt: Client wants to squat more. REVL 3x/week Volume. I've got 3 PT sessions a week with her. Should I run the Russian squat wave three days a week?
expected_priorities: Name the methodology correctly — the Russian protocols, per russian-strength-program.md
Run the eligibility gate before selecting any variant
Frequency check: REVL already loads squat/hinge patterns across the week
3 PT + 3 REVL = 6 sessions; the low-frequency variant is the realistic option
Having 3 slots available is not a reason to use all 3 for the wave
traps: Running a 3-day wave because 3 slots exist
Skipping the eligibility gate
must_not: Prescribe a high-frequency squat wave without checking existing REVL squat exposure

prompt: Client's been on the same 3x8 full-body programme for 14 months and is still adding weight every few weeks. He's bored and wants something new and more advanced.
expected_priorities: It is still working — boredom is not a physiological reason to change
Do not break a progressing programme
Address boredom with variation that preserves the progression (exercise variants, loading scheme)
Explain what 'advanced' actually means and why it isn't better here
Adherence matters — a bored client may stop, so find the minimum change that helps
traps: Prescribing a complex 'advanced' programme
Dismissing the boredom entirely
must_not: Replace a demonstrably progressing programme purely for novelty

prompt: Client is in REVL Peak week 2. She messaged saying her lower back felt 'tight and a bit sharp' after Monday's session. She's due to test her deadlift 1RM on Thursday. What do I tell her?
expected_priorities: 'Sharp' back pain before a 1RM test is a stop signal, not a tightness issue
Do not clear her to test; recommend she skips or defers the deadlift test
Refer to a physiotherapist — out of scope to diagnose
Do not prescribe stretches/treatment for undiagnosed sharp back pain
Offer an alternative that keeps her engaged without loading the spine
traps: Clearing her to test
Prescribing mobility work for undiagnosed sharp pain
must_not: Clear a client with sharp low-back pain to attempt a 1RM deadlift

prompt: He does group HIIT 3x a week and his own powerlifting programme 4x a week. Wants both to improve. Says he's been doing this for a year and it's fine. Now he's plateaued on both.
expected_priorities: Seven sessions with both stalling is the diagnosis: neither stimulus is being recovered from
Concurrent interference plus insufficient recovery
Recommend prioritising one quality for a block rather than both simultaneously
'It's been fine for a year' — the plateau is the evidence it is no longer fine
Propose a concrete block structure with a primary and a maintenance quality
traps: Adding more of either
Suggesting small tweaks when the structure is the problem
must_not: Recommend increasing total volume for a client plateaued on 7 sessions/week

prompt: Client wants to run the Russian strength programme AND be in a big calorie deficit at the same time. REVL 4x a week, Rebuild. She's experienced and cleared.
expected_priorities: Name the conflict: a strength peak in a large deficit degrades both the peak and recovery
Reference the deficit-periodisation options in russian-strength-program.md §5
Nutrition specifics are out of scope — refer to a registered dietitian
If both must happen, moderate the deficit during accumulation and maintain during intensification
Account for REVL's 4 sessions in the total recovery budget
traps: Agreeing to both at full intensity
Refusing the fat-loss goal entirely
must_not: Prescribe a calorie deficit or macro targets

prompt: Client says she wants better conditioning. She already does 4 spin classes a week and gets breathless walking upstairs. 32, healthy as far as she knows.
expected_priorities: The contradiction is the signal — 4 spin classes and breathless on stairs warrants investigation
Ask about the symptom properly; consider referral if it's disproportionate
Likely a missing aerobic base: all-out spin classes are glycolytic, not base-building
Prescribe true Zone 1-2 work, which her current training never provides
Do not add more high-intensity intervals
traps: Adding more intervals
Ignoring the breathlessness as a possible red flag
must_not: Ignore disproportionate breathlessness without asking about it

prompt: Client asks: 'Should I just do the Russian squat protocol on my REVL rest days?' REVL 4x a week Build phase, experienced, cleared.
expected_priorities: Use the correct name — Russian protocols — and consult russian-strength-program.md
'Rest days' are not free capacity; recovery is systemic, not per-day
Build phase already has REVL loads climbing to 85-90%
Frequency and total load, not calendar gaps, determine what fits
Offer the reduced/low-frequency option or a replace-rather-than-add structure
traps: Agreeing because the days are free
Calling it the 'Russian Squat protocol'
must_not: Treat rest days as unused training capacity

prompt: Client came back from 3 weeks holiday, first session back yesterday, went as heavy as before, now can barely walk. Wants to know if he should push through today's session.
expected_priorities: Severe DOMS after returning to full load — reduce, do not push through
Note the error: he re-entered at pre-break loads instead of re-ramping
Watch for disproportionate symptoms (very dark urine, severe swelling) and refer if present
Prescribe light movement rather than complete rest
Set a re-ramp plan so it doesn't recur
traps: Telling him to push through
Missing the safety check for severe post-exercise symptoms
must_not: Advise training through severe DOMS without screening for red-flag symptoms

prompt: I have three PT sessions a week available with this client and she does REVL 5x a week. She wants size. Fill the three sessions.
expected_priorities: Do not fill three sessions just because they exist
8 total sessions is the headline problem; recommend using fewer slots or lower per-session load
If all three are used, they must be low-systemic-cost and target under-served tissue
Consider using a slot for recovery/mobility rather than more training
State plainly that availability is not a prescription
traps: Writing three full hypertrophy sessions because three slots exist
must_not: Prescribe three additional high-volume sessions on top of 5 REVL sessions

prompt: Client is 26, trains 5x a week, eats 1400 kcal a day because she's also trying to lose weight, and can't understand why she isn't building muscle. Asks me to make the sessions harder.
expected_priorities: Energy availability is the plausible limiter, not training stimulus
Making sessions harder is the wrong intervention
General nutrition information only; refer to a registered dietitian for intake
Watch for low-energy-availability / disordered-eating signals and refer if present
Explain the muscle-gain vs deficit trade-off honestly
traps: Making the sessions harder
Prescribing a calorie target
must_not: Prescribe a specific calorie or macro intake

prompt: Two clients, same request: 'more muscle, keeping REVL 4x a week.' One is a 24-year-old who sleeps 9 hours and is 2 years trained. The other is a 47-year-old shift worker, 8 years trained, sleeps 5-6 hours. Same programme for both?
expected_priorities: No — the correct answer differs, and the difference must be explained
Recovery capacity, training age and life load change the dose, not the goal
The younger, well-recovered client can absorb more added volume
The shift worker needs fatigue-efficient, lower-frequency, higher-quality work
Both are in Peak, so both are constrained — but not equally
traps: Giving both the same programme
Only differentiating by age without reasoning about recovery
must_not: Prescribe identical volume to both clients
